4dc33674e3ba0c79:
**Split, so not a fusion** (`soup.split`, E). Bijective translations turn both bridges into one-operation laws: law 1 makes every left translation of · a bijection, and law 2 does the same for the right translations of ∘. E proves both directions of the equivalence with V(·) plus V^op(∘), where V = {x·(x·y) = y, (x·y)·y = y} (ETP 16 and 28) and V^op = {(x∘y)∘y = x, x∘(x∘y) = x}.

Nearest literature: bikei (involutory biquandles; Nelson and Rosenfield, arXiv:1603.02719, Definition 1). Their laws (ii.i) (x b y) b y = x and (ii.ii) (x a y) a y = x also make translations involutions. The candidate is not a bikei fragment: their Example 1 bikei (x a y = x b y = σ(x), σ an involution) fails x·(x·y) = y under either assignment of the operations. Searches (22 Nov 2026) found no source for V.
8a5129571ae99c51:
**An idempotent left quasigroup in disguise.** E proves both directions of the equivalence with {x·(y∘x) = y, (x·y)∘x = y, x·x = x, (x·y)·y = y, x·(y·x) = y·x}. So y∘x is the left division x\y of ·, and the theory is the variety of idempotent left quasigroups (·, \) satisfying x·(y·x) = y·x (ETP 333) and (x·y)·y = y (ETP 28). `soup.relabel` finds the same thing, up to relabelling, against the named left quasigroups. Rank 9 (`977c3603`) is the same without (x·y)·y = y.

Not a rack: E saturates against left distributivity. It is also not a twisted Ward left quasigroup ((x·y)·(x·z) = (y·y)·(y·z); Stanovský and Vojtěchovský, arXiv:2002.02854) and not a cycle set ((x·y)·(x·z) = (y·x)·(y·z), Rump 2005). The 3-element model is still a quandle: L₀ = L₁ = id, L₂ = (0 1). The affine models x·y = a·x + b·y with a² = 0 and b = (1+a)⁻¹, for instance 2x + 3y on ℤ/4, are Alexander quandles. Left quasigroups as a variety, with their commutator theory: Bonatto, *Nilpotent left quasigroups*, arXiv:2204.04448. Searches (22 Nov 2026) found no source that names left quasigroups with x(yx) = yx.

Verdict: a subvariety of a named variety (left quasigroups), cut out by two one-operation laws. It is a candidate for a name only if those two identities matter in the left-quasigroup or Yang–Baxter literature, and we found no sign that they do.
977c360353464d4e: **An idempotent left quasigroup in disguise.** E proves both directions of the equivalence with {x·(y∘x) = y, (x·y)∘x = y, x·x = x, x·(y·x) = y·x}: idempotent left quasigroups (y∘x = x\y) with x·(y·x) = y·x (ETP 333). Rank 2 (`8a512957`) adds (x·y)·y = y. Not a rack, not twisted Ward, not a cycle set (E saturates on each). Sources: as for `8a512957`.
1ca933c1787842d0:
**A subvariety of the named absorption pairs** (`soup.relabel`, E): it implies both absorption pairs as written, x·(x∘y) = x, x∘(x·y) = x and x·(y∘x) = x, x∘(y·x) = x. E's convergent presentation (24 rules) also gives each operation x·x = x, x·(x·y) = x (ETP 9), (x·y)·x = x·y (ETP 377) and (x·y)·y = x·y (ETP 378). It adds the bridges (x·y)∘x = x·y, (x∘y)·x = x∘y and three-variable rules such as x·((x·y)∘z) = x. It is a subvariety of `3078949b` (rank 4): every rule of that system is in this one.

No associativity and no commutativity: E saturates against both. Nearest literature: skew lattices and their absorption variants (Leech, *Noncommutative Lattices*, 2020), which are associative. That absorption alone forces idempotence without associativity is known there. Searches (22 Nov 2026) found no source for these law sets.
3078949be3c74059: **A subvariety of the named right absorption pair** (`soup.relabel`, E): it implies x·(y∘x) = x and x∘(y·x) = x. By E's convergent presentation (12 rules) it is equivalent to: both operations idempotent; each satisfying x·(x·y) = x (ETP 9) and (x·y)·y = x·y (ETP 378); the right absorptions; and the bridges (x·y)∘x = x·y and (x∘y)·x = x∘y. No associativity, no commutativity (E saturates). `1ca933c1` (rank 3) is a subvariety. Nearest literature as for `1ca933c1`. No source found for this set.
2dc2750850548a58: **No named theory implied** under any of the 8 relabellings (`soup.relabel`). By E's convergent presentation (12 rules), · alone satisfies x·x = x, x·(y·x) = x (ETP 10), (x·y)·x = x (ETP 25), (x·y)·y = x·y (ETP 378) and x·(x·y) = x·y (ETP 323). ∘ alone satisfies only x∘x = x. The bridges say that w = x∘y satisfies w·x = x, x·w = w, w·y = w and y·w = y. Not split: a 2-element certificate exists. Literature: according to the search results, groupoids with (xy)x = x and x(yx) = x appear as dual pairs in work on idempotent groupoid varieties (Demonstratio Math. 1994, doi:10.1515/dema-1994-3-426; Czech. Math. J. 48 (1998)). We did not read these papers, and the results show no second operation. No source found for the theory.
10c98c4b5db2a4bd: **Transpose-orthogonality with a decoder, plus absorption.** E proves both directions of the equivalence with B ∪ {(x∘y)·x = x, x·(y∘x) = x, (x·y)∘x = x, x∘(y·x) = x}, where B = {(x·y)∘(y·x) = x, (x∘y)·(y∘x) = x}. B says that φ(x,y) = (x·y, y·x) is a bijection of A² whose inverse is (u,v) ↦ (u∘v, v∘u). So · is orthogonal to its transpose as a binary operation, and ∘ decodes the pair. B alone does not imply idempotence or the absorptions (E saturates), so the absorptions are what the search added. The four absorptions are one law, (x∘y)·x = x, with its images under the three dualities. All four are needed: for each proper subset, E saturates against the rest. For Latin squares, orthogonality to the transpose is self-orthogonality. Self-orthogonal Latin squares exist for every order except 2, 3 and 6 (Brayton, Coppersmith and Hoffman, Bull. AMS 80 (1974)). Here · is never Latin in a non-degenerate model: the theory proves x·(x·y) = x·y, so a bijective left translation would be the identity, and · would be the right projection. With ∘ = ·, B becomes Schröder's second law (xy)(yx) = x. According to the search results, that is one of Belousov's identities that make a quasigroup orthogonal to a parastrophe; we did not read the sources. Non-degenerate models up to isomorphism (Mace4): none on 2 or 3 elements, 2 on 4, 14 on 5, at least 214 on 6 (the search hit its cap), all idempotent. B alone has 40 on 3 elements. In the smallest one, x·y keeps the high bit of y, and its low bit is x₀ + x₁(1 + y₁) (elements as bit pairs). E saturates against associativity and commutativity of either operation. Searches (22 Nov 2026) found no source for B as a two-operation variety, nor for B with these absorptions.
87137d88931fec5c: **In the absorption family of ranks 3 and 4.** It implies both absorption pairs (`soup.relabel`, E). It is a proper subvariety of `3078949b`: E proves that theory's laws from it, and saturates on two of its own laws the other way. It is incomparable with `1ca933c1`: E saturates in both directions on some law. Neither operation is associative or commutative (E saturates). E's convergent presentation has 30 rules. Nearest literature as for `1ca933c1`. No source found.
c8e6ca60ec8974cb: **Split, so not a fusion.** E's convergent presentation (10 rules) has no bridge at all. Each operation satisfies x·x = x, x·(y·x) = x, (x·y)·x = x, (x·y)·y = x·y and x·(x·y) = x·y, the same one-operation theory as the · part of `2dc27508`. Its four bridges follow from those one-operation laws.
